justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I'd assume was the prevailing price level at the time of the forecast, anchored around $184–186. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of $184.5 was driven primarily by short-term momentum and mean-reversion tendencies, assuming no major overnight catalysts. The one-week estimate of $185.0 reflects a near-flat bias, acknowledging that weekly price changes in liquid equities or ETFs tend to be small in expectation even when uncertainty is wide. The one-month estimate of $186.0 incorporates a slight positive drift consistent with long-run equity risk premium expectations, but the increment is intentionally small because drift over a single month is economically modest relative to volatility.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which reflects the square-root-of-time scaling of uncertainty under standard random walk assumptions. The one-day 90% interval of roughly plus or minus $5 corresponds to an implied daily volatility consistent with a moderately volatile asset. By one month, the interval spanning $163 to $210 reflects accumulated uncertainty over approximately 22 trading days, and also incorporates the possibility of regime changes, earnings announcements, or macro surprises that are harder to anticipate. The wider tails at longer horizons also reflect my uncertainty about the underlying volatility level itself, not just the price path.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden deterioration in macroeconomic conditions, a credit event, or a hawkish surprise from central banks could drive prices below $163 within a month. On the upside, a strong earnings beat, a dovish policy pivot, or a broad risk-on rally could push prices above $210. At the one-day horizon, a gap open following an after-hours announcement — whether a surprise earnings release, an index rebalancing event, or geopolitical news — could breach the $179–$190 range relatively easily.

It is also worth noting that my intervals assume reasonably continuous price behavior and normal market functioning. In stress scenarios — flash crashes, liquidity crises, or halts — the distribution of outcomes becomes fat-tailed in ways that standard volatility-based intervals do not capture well. The stated 90% intervals should therefore be understood as describing the central bulk of expected outcomes under relatively normal conditions, not as hard bounds on what is possible.
